evaluated.name: Cheap And Internally Funded Investment
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 1), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms that fund whatever they invest out of internal resources, rather than by issuing debt or equity, are disciplined allocators; expensive firms tapping external capital markets to finance expansion are the classic overvalued-equity-issuance combination.
evaluated.reasoning: External finance raised (change in long-term debt plus stock issuance, scaled by assets) is the funding-side counterpart of aggressive investment and is precisely when managers exploit high valuations, so pairing it with earnings yield captures the mispricing channel directly. COALESCE treats unreported issuance proceeds as zero, which is the economically correct convention for firms with no equity issuance in the year. The mechanism differs from asset-growth screens because it identifies who paid for the growth.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expensive Empire Builder Short
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), RANK(ADD(GROWTH(at, 1), RATIO(COALESCE(aqc, 0), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The most reliable half of the interaction is the short side: firms with rich market-to-book multiples that simultaneously expand organically and through acquisitions systematically disappoint as overvalued growth narratives.
evaluated.reasoning: Multiplying the market-to-book rank by the rank of total expansion intensity (asset growth plus acquisition spending) makes the signal large only when high price expectations and empire-building coincide, isolating the overvaluation-plus-overinvestment corner of the joint distribution. Including aqc separately captures inorganic expansion that asset growth alone can understate for serial acquirers, with unreported acquisitions set to zero. High values should predict low future returns, giving a negative expected slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Maintenance Adjusted Free Cash Flow Yield
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, MA(capx, 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What investors underprice is cash flow that survives the capital spending needed to sustain the business; a high yield on cash flow net of normalized capital expenditure identifies cheap firms whose investment program is modest, while heavy investors have their apparent cheapness eliminated by the deduction.
evaluated.reasoning: Netting three-year average capex out of operating cash flow before scaling by market capitalization embeds investment intensity inside the valuation multiple with market cap—always strictly positive—as the only denominator, which removes the explosive behavior of dividing by a near-zero capex/at. The 3-year moving average treats capex as a normalized maintenance requirement rather than a lumpy annual number, so the signal ranks firms by durable distributable cheapness instead of by inverse capex intensity. It remains a true interaction because the same operating-cash-flow yield maps to very different signal values depending on the firm's investment burden.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral EBITDA Yield Over Capacity Investment Rate
evaluated.expression: SUB(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, MA(ppegt, 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within an industry, firms priced cheaply on operating earnings while reinvesting at a low rate relative to their installed capacity base are disciplined operators the market extrapolates too pessimistically; peers with rich multiples and high capacity reinvestment rates are overvalued growth stories that will face overcapacity and falling returns on capital.
evaluated.reasoning: The sign is now stated consistently with the expression: high values mean cheap-and-restrained and predict high returns, low values mean expensive-and-expanding and predict low returns, so the Fama-MacBeth slope should be positive and the long-minus-short FF5 alpha positive. Replacing gross-PPE growth with the capex-to-average-gross-PPE reinvestment rate measures investment intensity relative to installed capacity rather than a one-year balance-sheet change, which is less mechanically related to CMA's asset-growth construction. Industry z-scoring of both legs removes the strong sector clustering in EBITDA multiples and capital intensity so the spread is a firm-level interaction, not a sector bet.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Value Premium Flip Across Capacity Growth Regimes
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), SUB(INDICATOR(NEG(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), -0.02), INDICATOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 0.15)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness carries opposite information in opposite capacity regimes: among firms holding gross physical capacity flat, a low price signals unrecognized capital discipline and predicts high returns, while among firms adding capacity above 15% per year a low price signals a value trap funding low-return expansion and predicts low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Because the regime weight flips the sign of the valuation z-score, the long leg (cheap, flat capacity) and the short leg (cheap, fast-expanding, plus expensive flat-capacity names) carry similar book-to-market exposure, so the HML loading largely cancels and any spread must come from the interaction itself — exactly the residual FF5 alpha the gen-0 additive signals lacked. Gross PPE growth is investment-exclusive and measures committed physical capacity rather than balance-sheet size, keeping it distinct from CMA's asset-growth construction. Firms in the 2%-15% middle band receive no view, which concentrates the tails on the economically interpretable corners.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capital Discipline Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value premium is not uniform: within the cheapest 30% of firms, those reinvesting at a low rate relative to installed net plant are genuinely disciplined and underpriced, while cheap firms plowing cash into their existing capital base are value traps whose price is low for a reason.
evaluated.reasoning: Conditioning on membership in the cheap group and then sorting only on reinvestment intensity makes both tails value-tilted, so the HML exposure of the long and short legs is matched and the spread isolates the value-trap discrimination channel rather than reproducing HML. The capex-to-net-PPE reinvestment rate is investment-exclusive and is a flow measure of capital deployment, which overlaps only partially with CMA's asset-growth factor. Zeros for the non-cheap 70% keep the extreme portfolios entirely inside the value group, which is the intended experiment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap And Cutting Reinvestment Conjunction
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm signals genuine capital discipline not by a low investment level but by actively reducing its reinvestment rate; when this turn toward restraint occurs in a cheaply priced firm, the market has not yet repriced the coming improvement in free cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning: The minimum of two ranks is an AND gate, so the top of the distribution contains only firms that are simultaneously cheap and cutting reinvestment, a strictly non-linear combination that no weighted sum of HML and CMA can reproduce. Using the one-year change in the capex-to-net-PPE rate rather than its level makes the investment leg a deceleration concept that CMA, a level-of-investment factor, should not absorb — the specific reason gen-0 level-based signals lost their alpha. Both inputs come from universally reported items, so coverage should be comparable to the gen-0 archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap With Rising Labor Productivity
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), GROWTH(RATIO(sale, emp), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment discipline shows up in the workforce as well as in plant: firms that raise revenue per employee are extracting more output from existing labor capacity instead of hiring into growth, and when such operating discipline coexists with a high EBITDA yield the market is underpricing an improving, self-funding business.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the economic channel from capital expenditure to labor input, a dimension of investment that neither CMA nor any capex-based control captures, so its predictive content has a better chance of surviving the five-factor benchmark. Revenue per employee growth is a productivity-of-investment measure rather than a quantity-of-investment measure, which distinguishes it from every gen-0 construction. Employment is broadly reported in Compustat, so coverage should not deteriorate relative to the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inorganic Versus Organic Expansion Within Expensive Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.7), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(aqc, 0), capx), at)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among richly valued firms, what distinguishes destroyed value is not how much they invest but how: those expanding mainly by buying other companies rather than by building their own capacity are using an inflated multiple as acquisition currency, and they underperform equally expensive, equally investment-heavy peers that grow organically.
evaluated.reasoning:
The archived empire-builder signal failed because FF5 already prices the expensive-plus-high-investment corner through HML and CMA, so the residual flipped positive; this redesign holds both valuation and total investment intensity roughly constant across the legs and sorts only on the acquisition-versus-capex composition of that investment, a dimension no FF5 factor represents. Because the numerator is a difference of two spending flows, a firm with heavy organic capex sits at the bottom and a serial acquirer at the top, eliminating the aqc double-counting with asset growth that the critic flagged earlier. Unreported acquisitions are treated as zero, the correct convention for non-acquirers.
REASONING_NOTE: Assets are used only as a common size deflator; the economic content comes from aqc and capx.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Profit Growth Per Unit Of Capital Growth Amplified By Cheapness
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(GROWTH(ebitda, 1), GROWTH(ppent, 1)), RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment quality is revealed when operating profit grows faster than the capital base that produced it, and this evidence is most mispriced where the market has assigned the lowest multiple: cheap firms whose profits are outrunning their capital stock are underappreciated disciplined allocators, while cheap firms adding capital without profit are genuine value traps.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing DELTA(ebitda)/MA(capx,3) with the scale-free wedge between EBITDA growth and net-PPE growth removes the near-zero-capex denominator that made the previous version collapse into an inverse-investment-level (CMA) sort, so the signal now measures productivity of capital rather than quantity of capital. Dividing by the cross-sectional rank of market-to-book — a strictly positive, bounded quantity — amplifies the wedge among cheap firms and compresses it toward zero among expensive ones, producing a multiplicative valuation-times-investment-quality interaction instead of the HML-dominated additive rank sum. Both inputs need only one annual lag, so coverage should be at least as good as the gen-0 archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Working Capital Buildup Weighted By Sales Yield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(GROWTH(RATIO(invt, sale), 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Inventory rising faster than sales is investment in working capital that has not yet been validated by demand, and this overinvestment is most damaging in firms already priced at high sales-to-price multiples, where the market is skeptical about demand in the first place.
evaluated.reasoning: Two things change relative to the gated family: the conditioning is continuous — the cheapness rank is a bounded positive weight that amplifies the discipline signal smoothly instead of switching it off — and the investment concept moves from fixed capital to working capital, which no FF5 factor represents. Comparing this against the hard-gated signals isolates whether the alpha comes from the conditioning shape or from the underlying interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Investment Instability Within Cheap Half
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(VOL(RATIO(capx, ppent), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital discipline is a process, not a level: among cheap firms, those whose reinvestment rate is stable year to year are running a predictable harvesting strategy, while those whose capital spending swings erratically are making opportunistic, poorly governed bets that the market underestimates the cost of.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the batch's most distinct mechanism because it uses a second moment of investment rather than its level or change, a dimension that CMA cannot span by construction and that the archive has never tested. A three-year volatility window keeps coverage close to the archive's 0.12-0.13 range while still capturing spending erraticism, and the cheap-half gate preserves the leg-matching that has been the only reliable route to positive FF5 alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Asset Vintage Within Cheap Half
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(ppent, ppegt)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two cheap firms with identical current spending differ enormously in future capital needs: one whose plant is largely undepreciated has already paid for its capacity and can harvest cash for years, while one whose plant is nearly fully depreciated faces a looming replacement bill that the low multiple does not yet reflect.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the spending-rate dimension entirely and conditions on the *stock* state of the capital base — net-to-gross PPE is an asset-vintage measure, not an investment level, so it is orthogonal to CMA and to the archive's capx-intensity signals rather than a renormalization of them. The economic content is forward capital obligation: cheapness is genuine only when the assets backing it do not need to be rebuilt, which is a distinct claim from "cheap firms should spend less."
REASONING_NOTE: The cheap-half gate is retained only because it is the leg-matching device that produced the archive's sole positive FF5 alpha; the informational content is new.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout Versus Capex Allocation Split Weighted By Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(dvc, ADD(dvc, capx))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital discipline is best revealed by how management splits internally generated funds between shareholders and the plant: a firm devoting a high share of that allocation to dividends rather than capex is credibly committing to not reinvesting, and this commitment is most underpriced where the market already assigns a low multiple.
evaluated.reasoning:
The investment leg is a bounded allocation share, dividends over dividends-plus-capex, which is neither a growth rate nor a scaled level, so it sidesteps both the published asset-growth content and the wrong-signed capacity-growth evidence in the archive. Cheapness enters as a continuous bounded weight rather than a hard gate, so the discipline signal is amplified smoothly among value firms and compressed among glamour firms, keeping value exposure similar across the two tails.
REASONING_NOTE: The denominator is strictly positive whenever either dividends or capex is positive, so no explosive scaling arises.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex Claim On Internal Cash Within Cheap Half
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ADD(capx, ABS(oancf)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters to a value investor is not the size of the capital program but how much of the firm's own cash generation it consumes: a cheap firm whose capex absorbs nearly all internal cash flow has no distributable value behind its low price, while one whose capex takes a small share of cash flow is a genuine harvester.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces the published equity-issuance channel with an internal-funding-claim measure that ties investment directly to the cash flow the valuation multiple is supposed to capitalize, so the information is about the sustainability of cheapness rather than about external financing decisions already documented in the issuance literature. Bounding the ratio by putting capex in both numerator and denominator, with the absolute value of operating cash flow, prevents the near-zero-denominator explosion that ruined the gen-0 cash-yield-per-capex construction.
REASONING_NOTE: Scaled by internal cash rather than by assets or plant, so it is not a capital-intensity sort.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Serial Acquisition Spending Within Cheap Half
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(TS_SUM(COALESCE(aqc, 0), 3), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Value firms with weak organic prospects that respond by repeatedly buying other companies are diworsifying, and the three-year cumulative cash outlay on acquisitions identifies the serial acquirers among them; cheap firms that abstain are the disciplined allocators.
evaluated.reasoning:
Replacing the change in goodwill with cash acquisition outlays removes the impairment contamination the critic identified — aqc is a cash-flow-statement investing outflow that can only be positive spending, so the long leg no longer buys firms writing down past mistakes — and it is reported consistently across the full sample rather than only post-SFAS-142. Cumulating over three years targets serial acquisitiveness as a management style rather than a single lumpy deal, which is the behavioral trait the hypothesis is about, and zero is the economically correct value for non-acquirers.
REASONING_NOTE: Inorganic expansion remains a distinct channel from the organic capex measures already in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Reinvestment Discipline In Both Valuation Tails
evaluated.expression: MUL(ADD(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Reinvestment intensity is informative about returns only where price expectations are extreme — among deep-value firms it separates harvesters from value traps, and among glamour firms it separates asset-light compounders from empire builders — while for middling valuations capital spending carries no mispricing content.
evaluated.reasoning: This doubles the informative mass of the archive's best design from 30% to 60% of the universe, directly fixing the thin-tail and degenerate-breakpoint problem the critic identified, and it does so by adding an economically motivated second gate rather than by nudging a percentile. It is also a diagnostic: if alpha survives or strengthens, the interaction lives in both valuation tails; if it collapses, the mispricing is specific to the value side and future work should stay there.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Replacement Cost Cheapness With Reinvestment Restraint
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ppegt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness anchored on physical capacity — market value per dollar of gross installed plant, a crude replacement-cost multiple — identifies firms trading below the cost of rebuilding their asset base, and among these the ones not adding further capacity are the genuinely underappreciated disciplined operators.
evaluated.reasoning: This changes the valuation anchor from accounting book equity, which is distorted by write-downs, buybacks, and leverage, to gross physical capital at historical cost, so the gate now identifies low Tobin-q-on-capacity firms rather than low-book-to-price firms and the resulting long leg is not a repackaged HML portfolio. Because both the gate and the discriminator are built from investment-account variables while price supplies the valuation side, the signal is a genuine q-theory statement: cheap relative to installed capacity and refusing to add more.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Sweating Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), WINSOR(ZSCORE(GROWTH(RATIO(sale, ppegt), 1)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Disciplined allocation means getting more revenue out of the capacity you already own; among cheap firms, rising sales per dollar of gross plant signals management sweating existing assets instead of building new ones, and the market underestimates how much free cash that generates.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the utilization dimension rather than the spending dimension: the same low-capex firm can be starving a shrinking business or squeezing more output from installed capacity, and only the second is a disciplined allocator, so the signal targets a distinction the archive's level and change-in-level signals cannot make. It uses gross rather than net plant so the ratio is not mechanically inflated by depreciation, which is what corrupted the asset-vintage test that produced a wrong-signed slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Total Operating Capital Absorption Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(ADD(capx, DELTA(invt, 1)), ADD(ppent, invt))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What drains a cheap firm's distributable cash is the total capital it absorbs, fixed plus working, so the right discipline measure is combined capital absorption per dollar of operating capital already employed; firms with low total absorption are harvesters and those with high absorption are consuming the very cash flow the low multiple is supposed to represent.
evaluated.reasoning:
Instead of blending the ranks of two evaluated signals, this builds a single new accounting quantity — capex plus the change in inventory over plant plus inventory — which is the firm's total incremental claim on operating capital and is not the sum of two previously tested sorts. Because the denominator includes inventory, the measure is meaningful for distribution- and retail-type value firms whose capital is in stock rather than plant, extending the winning mechanism to firms where capx/ppent is uninformative, and no giant tie block enters the construction beyond the intended valuation gate.
REASONING_NOTE: Positive denominator by construction, so no explosive scaling.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capital Deepening Against Labor Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(GROWTH(RATIO(ppent, emp), 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Irreversibility is the cost of aggressive investment: a cheaply valued firm that raises capital per worker is substituting sunk, non-recoverable plant for flexible labor precisely when the market says its growth options are worth little, and it loses the ability to shrink cheaply if demand disappoints.
evaluated.reasoning:
The discriminator is the capital-labor mix, not the hiring rate — headcount growth enters the ratio with the opposite sign to plant growth, so a firm that hires while holding plant flat scores as disciplined here and as undisciplined under the employment-growth anomaly, which makes this a distinct and partly opposing prediction rather than a known factor conditioned on value. Framing discipline as commitment irreversibility also explains why the level of spending matters more for value firms, whose depressed multiples imply little option value in new capacity, and ratio-of-levels construction is less sensitive to stale or rounded employment counts than a headcount growth rate alone.
REASONING_NOTE: Uses plant per employee, so both the investment and the labor input enter as a single economic quantity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expansion Overhang Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(LAG(capx, 2), ppent)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The damage from aggressive investment is felt with a lag: a cheap firm whose heavy spending occurred two years ago is now carrying capacity built for demand that did not arrive, and that overhang depresses future margins and returns, whereas a cheap firm that was already restrained two years ago has no such legacy to absorb.
evaluated.reasoning:
This introduces a timing dimension the archive has never tested — every prior investment leg used contemporaneous levels or one-year changes — so the comparison with the archive's best signal directly identifies whether the mispricing is about current capital discipline or about the unrecognized legacy of past expansion, which is the economically more plausible story since capacity built earlier only shows up in realized profitability later. It is not a reweighting of the winner: past and current reinvestment rates are far from collinear, and the design deliberately allows a firm currently spending heavily to be classified as clean if its prior expansion was modest.
REASONING_NOTE: Only a two-year lag is required, so coverage should stay near the archive's 0.12-0.13 range.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expectation Deployment Congruence Product
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Returns are earned when a firm's capital deployment is congruent with the market's price expectations — a low multiple backed by capital restraint means genuine harvesting, and a high multiple backed by heavy reinvestment means the growth option is actually being exercised — while incongruent firms (cheap but still expanding, expensive but deploying nothing) are mispriced in the other direction.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's cheap-gate alpha of +4.2% and the two-tail alpha of −4.5% together imply the glamour-tail effect is large and opposite in sign, which is exactly the centered-product structure this expression implements; it is the functional form the evidence points to rather than a new economic story bolted on. Unlike gated designs it has no zero mass, so both extreme deciles are populated by economically interpretable corners and coverage stays at full archive levels.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Congruence With Lagged Capital Deployment
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(LAG(capx, 2), ppent)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Congruence is best judged against the spending that has already had time to show up in operations: a cheap firm that expanded two years ago carries unrecognized overcapacity, while an expensive firm whose earlier expansion is now maturing is delivering on the growth the multiple assumed.
evaluated.reasoning: This combines the archive's two largest alphas — the cheap-gate discipline signal at +4.2% and the two-year-lagged capex overhang signal at +5.1% (t=1.9) — inside the congruence form the sign evidence supports, so it tests whether the timing dimension and the functional form reinforce each other. The lag also mitigates the simultaneity concern that current capex and current price both respond to the same contemporaneous news, which should help the FMB slope that the overhang signal left weak at 1.27.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral Congruence Product
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), NEG(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Both cheapness and reinvestment intensity are strongly industry-determined — utilities are perpetually capital-hungry and low-multiple, software firms the reverse — so congruence should be judged against industry norms, comparing each firm to peers facing the same technology and the same typical multiple.
evaluated.reasoning: Without industry neutralization the raw product mechanically pairs capital-intensive value sectors on one side and asset-light glamour sectors on the other, so a large part of the spread could be a static sector bet that would be fragile out of sample; double industry z-scoring forces the interaction to be firm-specific. This also addresses the critic's standing concern that capital intensity is a technology characteristic rather than a discipline choice, and it should improve the FMB slope if the congruence effect is genuinely within-industry.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unvalidated Expansion Within Glamour Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3), WINSOR(ZSCORE(SUB(GROWTH(ppent, 1), GROWTH(ebitda, 1))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among the most richly valued firms, the ones whose capital base is growing faster than their operating profits are expanding without validation — the multiple already prices growth that the income statement is not delivering — while expensive firms whose profits are outrunning their capital base are genuinely converting expansion into earnings.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the back-fitted claim that heavy investment per se is good among glamour firms and replaces it with a sign that agrees with the investment anomaly: expansion is penalized, but only the portion unmatched by profit growth, which is the economically meaningful part. Both legs of the spread sit inside the expensive tail, so the growth tilt is matched and the spread cannot be a repackaged short-HML position; the discriminator is a capital-versus-profit wedge, not a capex level, so it is also not spanned by CMA.
REASONING_NOTE: The gate selects the cheapest-30%-complement, i.e. book-to-market rank below 0.3.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Adaptation To Own Repricing
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5)), 1), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(DELTA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is whether management adapts its capital plan to the market's revised verdict on the firm: a firm now cheap relative to its own five-year valuation history that responds by cutting its reinvestment rate is adapting and will be rewarded, whereas one that keeps raising investment in the face of its own derating is in denial and will disappoint.
evaluated.reasoning:
The valuation leg is a firm-specific repricing state — position of current book-to-market within its own five-year range — which separates newly derated firms from permanently cheap industries, a distinction no cross-sectional multiple can make and one that HML cannot span. Pairing it with the change in the reinvestment rate makes the mechanism managerial responsiveness rather than the level of cheapness or the level of investment, so both legs of the interaction are dynamic and the design is not a re-encoding of the level-based congruence product.
REASONING_NOTE: A five-year window on an annual ratio plus one capex lag keeps coverage near the archive's range while capturing the repricing state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft Asset Bloat Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all asset expansion is capacity: for cheap firms the most damaging growth is in non-physical operating assets — receivables, inventory, acquired intangibles — which represents bloat and soft accounting rather than productive capacity, while cheap firms holding these assets flat are running a tight operation.
evaluated.reasoning:
Replacing acquisition outlays with the change in non-cash, non-plant operating assets removes the degeneracy the critic identified — that leg is continuously distributed across essentially all firms instead of being zero for most of them, so the signal can never collapse into plain book-to-market. It also isolates a channel the archive has not tested: physical capacity expansion and soft-asset expansion are economically different, and the value-matched gate keeps both spread legs inside the cheap group so the alpha cannot come from a value tilt.
REASONING_NOTE: Cash is subtracted so that hoarding liquidity is not counted as investment, and net plant is subtracted so the measure is orthogonal to the capex channel already in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unvalidated Expansion Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(SUB(GROWTH(ppent, 1), GROWTH(ebitda, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The wedge between capital growth and operating profit growth measures expansion the business has not earned, and it should identify value traps just as sharply as it identifies hollow growth stories: a cheap firm growing its plant faster than its profits is destroying the free cash its low multiple implies.
evaluated.reasoning: The glamour-tail version of this exact discriminator produced the archive's cleanest triple result (FMB −3.17, alpha −3.5%, t=−2.83), so the highest-value next test is whether the same wedge works in the value tail where the leg-matched gate has already produced positive alpha with other discriminators. The wedge is scale-free and jointly uses profitability and capital, so it is not spanned by CMA and cannot be a repackaged capital-intensity sort.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Persistent Soft Asset Bloat Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 3), LAG(at, 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Bloat in non-cash, non-plant operating assets is damaging when it is a persistent multi-year accumulation rather than a single-year fluctuation, because sustained buildup of receivables, inventory, and acquired intangibles reflects a business model that quietly consumes capital while its low multiple suggests otherwise.
evaluated.reasoning: The one-year version of this discriminator is the archive's best joint result (FMB 2.83, alpha +3.7%, t=2.65), and the separate expansion-overhang evidence (alpha +5.1% on two-year-lagged capex) says multi-year measurement of investment carries more return-relevant information than the current year, so the timing axis is the highest-value refinement available. A three-year change also averages out working-capital seasonality and one-off acquisitions, which should raise the FMB t-stat rather than merely the alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral Soft Asset Bloat Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Normal rates of working-capital and intangible-asset growth differ sharply across industries — distributors and pharma acquirers naturally carry high soft-asset growth — so bloat that signals mismanagement must be judged relative to industry peers rather than the whole market.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's best signal has a raw Sharpe of −0.10 despite a strong FF5 alpha, which is the signature of a spread whose raw return is offset by a persistent sector or factor tilt; industry z-scoring the discriminator is the diagnostic and the likely fix, since it removes the static sector composition while leaving the firm-level bloat information intact. If both the FMB slope and the alpha t-stat improve, future work should be industry-neutral throughout.

evaluated.name: Soft Asset Bloat Within Glamour Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensive firms accumulating non-cash, non-plant operating assets are capitalizing growth into the balance sheet without the cash flow to show for it, and this soft expansion should predict underperformance among glamour names just as unvalidated plant growth does.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the mirror experiment to Signal 2 and completes a clean 2x2 of the archive's two best discriminators against the two valuation tails, which is the cheapest way to learn whether these mispricings are tail-specific or general before committing the remaining generations. The gate keeps both spread legs inside the expensive group, so a negative alpha here cannot be a disguised short-HML position.

evaluated.name: Expansion Share Of Capital Spending Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(ppent, 1), ADD(capx, ABS(DELTA(ppent, 1))))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital spending splits into replacement of consumed plant and genuine expansion, and only the expansion portion is a discretionary bet; since the change in net plant equals capex less depreciation, the share of total capital activity that ends up enlarging the net asset base identifies the true expanders among cheap firms, while firms whose spending merely offsets wear-and-tear are neutral harvesters.
evaluated.reasoning:
This implements the accounting identity the critique asked for — net investment, not accumulated depreciation — so it measures spending net of annual wear-and-tear instead of asset vintage, and it therefore does not overlap the failed net-to-gross plant signal. Placing the absolute net investment in the denominator alongside capex bounds the ratio between −1 and 1, eliminating the near-zero-denominator instability that would afflict either a capex-only or a depreciation-only scaling.
REASONING_NOTE: Firms shrinking their net plant score negative, i.e. maximally disciplined, which is the intended economic ordering.

evaluated.name: Working Capital Bloat Excluding Intangibles Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), COALESCE(intan, 0)), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The soft-asset result should be driven by operating bloat that management controls directly — receivables extended to weak customers and inventory built ahead of demand — rather than by purchased intangibles, because working-capital expansion reflects deteriorating business quality while intangible additions reflect discrete acquisition decisions.
evaluated.reasoning: Stripping intangibles out of the winning discriminator is a direct attribution test: if the alpha survives, the mechanism is operating-cycle bloat and future work should refine working capital; if it collapses, the mechanism is acquisitive growth and the design should switch to acquisition measures. It also removes the goodwill-impairment contamination that made earlier intangible-based proposals uninterpretable, since write-downs no longer enter the measure at all.

evaluated.name: Demand Validated Soft Asset Bloat Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Soft assets growing in line with revenue are simply the working capital a growing business requires, whereas soft assets outgrowing revenue are genuine bloat, so scaling the expansion against demand rather than against total assets should isolate the value-destroying portion.
evaluated.reasoning: The analogous validation test using EBITDA growth failed badly in the cheap tail (FMB −0.56) even though it works in the glamour tail, and the natural explanation is that profit growth for value firms is dominated by margin noise and one-off charges while revenue growth is a stable measure of the capital a business genuinely needs. If the sales-validated wedge succeeds where the profit-validated wedge failed, the lesson is that the correct benchmark for expansion is demand, not earnings.

evaluated.name: Cash Yield Gated Soft Asset Bloat
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness measured by operating cash flow relative to price identifies firms that actually generate distributable cash, unlike high book-to-market which also captures distressed and written-down balance sheets, so bloat discipline should be more informative among genuinely cash-cheap firms.
evaluated.reasoning: Every gated design in the archive uses the same book-based gate, so it is untested whether the alpha requires book-to-market specifically or merely a valuation-matched conditioning set; substituting a cash-flow-yield gate answers that and simultaneously screens out the distress contamination that plausibly explains why these spreads have strong alphas but near-zero raw Sharpe ratios. If the alpha improves, the gate itself — not just the discriminator — becomes a target for the final refinements.

evaluated.name: Soft Asset Bloat Across Both Valuation Tails
evaluated.expression: MUL(ADD(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Soft-asset bloat predicts underperformance with the same sign in both valuation tails — cheap bloaters are value traps and expensive bloaters are capitalizing growth they cannot fund from cash — so conditioning on extreme valuation of either kind, rather than on cheapness alone, should double the informative breadth without sign cancellation.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the reinvestment-intensity discriminator, whose two-tail extension reversed the alpha to −4.5%, the bloat discriminator has now been shown to have a correctly signed and even stronger FMB slope in the glamour tail (−3.86), so the two tails should reinforce rather than offset and the pooled design is a genuine test of breadth rather than a repeat of a known failure. The result also discriminates the two competing readings of the archive: that valuation gating works because value firms are special, or that it works because mispricing concentrates wherever price expectations are extreme.

evaluated.name: Deteriorating Capital Efficiency Trend Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), sale), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What condemns a cheap firm is not the size of one year's soft-asset build but a persistent structural drift in how much non-cash operating capital it needs per dollar of revenue; a rising multi-year trend in that requirement means the business model is quietly becoming more capital-hungry, which the low multiple has not priced.
evaluated.reasoning:
This is a different economic object rather than a horizon interpolation: the discriminator is the fitted slope of an efficiency *ratio* — soft operating assets per dollar of sales — so a firm growing soft assets in proportion to a growing business registers no signal at all, whereas both the one-year and three-year change measures would flag it. It therefore tests structural deterioration of the operating model instead of the magnitude of recent accumulation, and it also nests a demand benchmark inside the discriminator rather than beside it.
REASONING_NOTE: The five-year window is required for a meaningful slope; coverage should land near the archive's three-year variants at roughly 0.10.

evaluated.name: Simultaneous Restraint Conjunction Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), MIN(NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Genuine capital discipline must hold on both fronts at once: a cheap firm earns the harvester label only if it is simultaneously restrained in plant spending and in soft-asset accumulation, because a firm restrained on just one dimension is typically relocating expansion to the other part of the balance sheet rather than returning cash.
evaluated.reasoning:
The minimum of the two restraint scores implements the conjunction the hypothesis asserts — a firm is scored by its weaker dimension, so extreme restraint in plant cannot offset soft-asset bloat, which is exactly what the additive version wrongly permitted. This makes the signal a genuine non-linear AND gate over two orthogonal balance-sheet channels, and the short tail identifies firms expanding on at least one front, testing the substitution story that neither component alone can address.
REASONING_NOTE: All ranking is done inside the cheap tail's gate, so both spread legs retain matched value exposure.

evaluated.name: Profitable Value Gated Soft Asset Bloat
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(ib, 0)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Balance-sheet discipline is only interpretable in a firm that has earnings to allocate; among loss-making deep-value firms, changes in operating assets reflect forced liquidation and distress dynamics rather than management's capital-allocation choices, so screening them out should sharpen the bloat signal on both the cross-sectional and portfolio dimensions.
evaluated.reasoning: Every gated design in the archive has a strong FF5 alpha but a raw Sharpe near zero, the classic signature of a spread whose extremes are populated by distressed micro-caps whose returns are noisy in both directions; requiring positive income is an economically motivated purification of the conditioning set rather than a percentile tweak. If both the FMB slope and the alpha t-stat rise while coverage stays near 0.10, the final generations should adopt the profitable-value gate as the standard container.

evaluated.name: Three Year Working Capital Bloat Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), COALESCE(intan, 0)), 3), LAG(at, 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The two independent findings about the winning discriminator — that the working-capital component carries the cross-sectional slope and that multi-year accumulation carries the abnormal return — should reflect the same underlying phenomenon, namely a slow, management-controlled build-up of receivables and inventory that erodes cash generation without appearing in the income statement.
evaluated.reasoning: The attribution test raised the FMB slope to 2.94 by removing intangibles, and the horizon test raised the alpha to +5.1% by extending to three years; if these are two views of one mechanism the combination should dominate both parents, and if instead they are separate effects the combination will be no better, which is itself decisive information for the final generation. Excluding intangibles also removes the impairment and acquisition contamination that makes multi-year balance-sheet differences hard to interpret.

evaluated.name: Own History Abnormal Bloat Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms differ permanently in how much operating capital their business model requires, so what signals indiscipline is a build-up that is unusual *for that firm* — a soft-asset expansion at the top of its own five-year range — rather than one that is merely large relative to other companies.
evaluated.reasoning: The cross-sectional z-score of bloat conflates a distributor that always carries growing receivables with a firm that has just started stuffing its balance sheet, and the own-history rank removes that permanent component without industry classification, which the industry-neutral variant attempted and only partly achieved (alpha fell to +2.2%). This is a different normalization concept from horizon or industry adjustment — a within-firm benchmark — and it directly targets the noise most likely to be depressing the alpha t-statistic.

evaluated.name: Soft Expansion Unmatched By Profit Within Glamour Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3), WINSOR(ZSCORE(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), GROWTH(ebitda, 1))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: In the glamour tail the damaging pattern is expansion the income statement does not validate, and it should apply to soft operating assets exactly as it does to plant: an expensive firm whose receivables, inventory, and intangibles grow faster than its operating profit is capitalizing a growth story into the balance sheet instead of earning it.
evaluated.reasoning: The glamour tail has produced only two tests, and both worked in the cross-section — the plant-versus-profit wedge with alpha −3.5% (t=−2.83) and raw bloat with FMB −3.86 — so combining the profit-validation benchmark that generated glamour-side alpha with the soft-asset measure that generated the strongest glamour-side slope is the highest-value remaining experiment on that side. Both legs stay inside the expensive 30%, so a negative alpha cannot be a disguised short-value position, and success would give the final generation a genuine two-sided strategy rather than a value-only one.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Build Against Revenue Base Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(invt, 0), 1), LAG(sale, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Inventory is the one soft asset whose correct size is dictated by expected demand, so a cheap firm adding inventory relative to the revenue base it must serve is revealing a demand forecast the market does not share, and the resulting markdowns and cash absorption are not yet in the price.
evaluated.reasoning:
This tests the inventory channel on its own economic terms — scaled by the prior-year revenue that inventory exists to support rather than by total assets — instead of forming a residual after subtracting components, which is what made the previous version both a third re-slicing and a sample-biasing construction. Treating unreported inventory as zero is the economically correct convention for service and financial-type firms, which genuinely hold none, so the measure is defined across the whole cheap tail and coverage should match the archive's 0.12-0.13 range.
REASONING_NOTE: If this succeeds while the intangibles-excluded version also succeeds, the mechanism is demand misjudgment; if only the broader measure works, inventory is not the driver.

evaluated.name: Bloat Share Of Cash Activity Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), ADD(ABS(oancf), ABS(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The funding consequence of soft-asset accumulation is best expressed as a share: when the operating asset build is large relative to the total cash activity of the firm, the build must be financed rather than absorbed, whereas when internal cash generation dwarfs the build the same expansion is self-funded and harmless.
evaluated.reasoning:
Normalizing the build by the sum of the absolute cash flow and the absolute build bounds the discriminator between −1 and 1 and makes it scale-free in both arguments, so it cannot be dominated by the level of oancf/assets and therefore cannot degenerate into a cash-flow profitability sort inside a value gate — the identification problem the critique correctly raised. What the slope now identifies is the relative weight of balance-sheet absorption versus cash generation, which is the funding-gap concept the hypothesis asserts.
REASONING_NOTE: The absolute values keep the denominator strictly positive for any firm with either nonzero cash flow or a nonzero build, so no explosive scaling or sign inversion arises.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Conversion Of Operating Assets Into Cash Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(che, 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1)), LAG(at, 1))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: A disciplined cheap firm does not merely avoid bloat, it actively converts operating assets into cash — collecting receivables, running down inventory, and letting the proceeds sit in liquid form — and that transformation of illiquid working capital into distributable cash is exactly what a depressed multiple fails to anticipate.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has always excluded cash from the discriminator to avoid treating hoarding as investment, but that discards the informative contrast between a firm whose asset base shrinks into cash and one whose asset base shrinks through write-offs; differencing the two flows tests the liquidity-conversion channel directly. It also gives the long leg a positive economic identity — cash generation — instead of merely the absence of expansion, which may finally produce a spread with a positive raw return rather than pure factor offset.

evaluated.name: Average Annual Bloat Rate Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(MA(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1)), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Chronic bloat is best measured as the average of three consecutive annual accumulation rates, each scaled by the asset base in force at the time, because that captures a persistent habit of absorbing capital without letting a single stale denominator or one endpoint year dominate the measure.
evaluated.reasoning: The three-year endpoint difference produced the archive's largest alpha (+5.1%) but its weakest FMB slope among the strong variants (2.39), a pattern consistent with endpoint noise and a three-year-old denominator; averaging the annual rates keeps the same three-year economic content while measuring each year against its own base. This is the one refinement that could plausibly deliver the multi-year alpha and the one-year slope simultaneously, which is precisely what the final generation needs.

evaluated.name: Materiality Of Bloat Per Dollar Of Market Value Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms the market already values cheaply, what matters is how large the operating-asset build is relative to shareholder value rather than relative to the accounting asset base: a build worth a tenth of market capitalization absorbs a tenth of what shareholders own, while the same build at a firm with a large asset base but similar price is far less consequential.
evaluated.reasoning:
Restoring the validated cheap gate removes the mechanical value tilt the critique identified, because all firms carrying a nonzero score already sit in the top book-to-market tercile, so residual variation in the price deflator across the spread legs is small and the ranking is driven by build size rather than by cheapness. What remains is a genuine change in economic content relative to the archive: the deflator is shareholder value rather than book assets or sales, so the discriminator measures the materiality of the build to owners, which is the quantity the mispricing story is actually about.
REASONING_NOTE: Coverage should match the archive's gated variants at roughly 0.13 since no additional lags are required.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Bloat Against The Equity Cushion Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(ceq, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The danger of soft-asset accumulation depends on the equity cushion that must absorb it: for a levered cheap firm, a build equal to a fifth of book equity can wipe out its solvency margin if the receivables prove uncollectible or the inventory must be marked down, whereas the same build against a large unlevered equity base is easily absorbed.
evaluated.reasoning:
Deflating by book equity rather than total assets automatically scales the discriminator up for levered firms, so the measure embeds a solvency-risk interaction that no asset-scaled variant in the archive captures — this is economic content, not the sample screen the size-based proposal amounted to. It also gives a testable prediction distinct from the existing family: if the bloat effect is really about the fragility of the equity cushion, the equity-deflated version should dominate the asset-deflated one, and if it is purely about capital absorption the two should perform alike.
REASONING_NOTE: Firms with negative book equity are excluded by the value gate's construction, so the deflator stays positive where the signal is active.

evaluated.name: Bloat Among Firms Cheap Three Years Running
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(RANK(LAG(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 3)), 0.7)), NEG(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that was already in the cheapest tercile three years ago and remains there today has received a settled verdict from the market, and continued accumulation of operating assets in that situation reveals managerial refusal to adapt rather than a transient working-capital swing — the freshly derated firms that a snapshot gate also captures are still in the middle of price discovery.
evaluated.reasoning:
Conditioning on the *lagged* valuation rank rather than a moving average that includes the current value avoids the collinearity the critique identified, since the three-year-old rank and today's rank differ materially: a large share of currently cheap firms were mid- or high-priced three years ago, and this construction excludes exactly those. The economic content is the persistence of price expectations as a state variable, which the archive has only probed through a failed continuous product design, never inside the gated structure that produces alpha.
REASONING_NOTE: The three-year lag on the valuation ratio should place coverage near 0.11, comparable to the archive's multi-year variants.

evaluated.name: Soft Expansion Among Low Profitability Glamour Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), -0.3), INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(ib, at))), -0.5)), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(at, 1))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: An expensive multiple is a promise about future returns on capital, so soft-asset expansion is least likely to be validated among expensive firms whose current returns on assets are already below the market median; those firms are enlarging a balance sheet that is not yet earning, and the market is paying in advance for growth that the existing asset base does not support.
evaluated.reasoning:
Replacing the negative-earnings screen with a below-median return-on-assets screen roughly triples the size of the conditioning cohort — about half of the expensive tercile rather than the small loss-making slice — which addresses the sparsity and distress-overlap concern while preserving the diagnosis that the broad glamour gate dilutes the short leg. Both spread legs remain inside the same expensive, low-profitability cohort, so a negative alpha cannot be a repackaged profitability or value factor exposure, and the discriminator is the same soft-asset build that produced the strongest glamour-side slope in the archive.
REASONING_NOTE: Using ib scaled by assets keeps the screen a profitability ranking rather than a sign test, avoiding the unstable behavior of loss indicators.

evaluated.name: Two Channel Discipline Sum Within Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), NEG(ADD(WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, che), ppent), 1), LAG(ceq, 1))), 1), WINSOR(ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, ppent)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Fixed-capital reinvestment and soft-asset accumulation are two largely independent ways for a cheap firm to consume capital, and since both have been shown to predict returns inside the value gate, total capital absorption across the two channels should be a more complete and less noisy measure of indiscipline than either alone.
evaluated.reasoning: The conjunctive MIN version of this pairing produced a weaker alpha (+2.4%) than either parent, which tells us discipline is not an all-or-nothing condition but a matter of degree, and the untested implication is that the two channels should be *summed* rather than gated against each other. Both components have alphas above 3% inside the identical value gate and are only weakly correlated with each other — capex intensity is a technology characteristic while soft-asset growth is an operating-cycle outcome — so averaging them should reduce measurement noise and lift the alpha t-statistic even if the alpha magnitude sits between the two parents.
